items.text: COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO RULES

items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the penal law, in relation to causing the death of a police or peace officer
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5849

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the penal law, in relation to causing the death of a
police or peace officer

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

This act shall be known as and may be cited as the "Police Officer
Vincent Guidice Memorial Act." This bill would amend Section 125.22 of
the Penal Law, aggravated manslaughter in the first degree, to make it
a class B felony to cause the death of a police officer or peace
officer, when the offender acts with intent to prevent such civil
servant from performing a lawful duty.

REASONS FOR SUPPORT:

On May 22, 1996, New York City Police Officer Vincent Guidice died
tragically as a result of serious injuries that he sustained in the
line of duty. Police Officer Guidice had responded to a report of
domestic violence and attempted to make an arrest. He struggled with
the suspect amid shards of glass from a broken mirror that had been
thrown upon the floor earlier in the domestic dispute. Office Guidice
died as a result of injuries he sustained during the struggle.

Subsequently, the Office of the Bronx County District Attorney filed
charges of manslaughter in the second degree and criminally negligent
homicide because the District Attorney concluded that the facts of the
case would not support a more serious charge. The Grand Jury
ultimately indicted the defendant on lesser charges including assault
in the second degree, a class D felony, as well as criminally
negligent homicide, a class E felony. Even though the Penal Law
charges of murder in the second degree or manslaughter in the first
degree could have been interpreted to include the facts of this case,
Officer Guidice's killer was charged only with a class D felony.
Because of the possibility of this kind of interpretation, the Penal
Law should be amended to make absolutely clear the consequences of
causing an officers death in this manner.

This legislation seeks to establish a homicide charge when an
officer's life is taken. However, it would not subject offenders to
capital punishment, which remains reserved for those who intentionally
cause death.

Accordingly, the Mayor urges the earliest possible favorable
consideration of this proposal by the Legislature.
